title: Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: A market has no arbitrage essentially if and only if there exists an equivalent martingale measure under which discounted asset prices are martingales.
latex: \text{no arbitrage}\iff \exists\ \mathbb Q\sim\mathbb P:\ e^{-rt}S_t\ \text{is a }\mathbb Q\text{-martingale}
short: Arbitrage-free prices are expectations under a risk-neutral measure.
long: Arbitrage-free prices are expectations under a risk-neutral measure. In incomplete markets the equivalent martingale measure need not be unique.
proof: Use the Hahn–Banach or separating hyperplane theorem to construct the pricing functional and show it defines a positive measure.
consequence: It links derivative pricing to martingale theory and completeness.

title: Put–Call Parity
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: For European options with the same strike and maturity and no dividends, the call price minus the put price equals the spot price minus the discounted strike.
short: A long call and short put replicate the underlying financed by borrowing.
long: A long call and short put replicate the underlying financed by borrowing. Dividends or foreign-currency carry modify the right-hand side by the present value of the dividend stream.
proof: At maturity both portfolios pay max(S_T-K,0)-max(K-S_T,0)=S_T-K; no-arbitrage then forces equality of initial values.
consequence: It detects arbitrage violations and links call and put markets.

title: Kalman Controllability Rank Condition
subject: Control Theory
statement: A finite-dimensional linear system is controllable exactly when the matrix formed from B, AB, ..., A^(n-1)B has full row rank.
short: Inputs must reach every mode of the system.
long: Inputs must reach every mode of the system. The condition is equivalent to the observability of the transposed dual system.
proof: If the rank is deficient, an eigenvector of A^T orthogonal to the reachable subspace cannot be influenced; conversely the Cayley–Hamilton theorem shows the reachable subspace is A-invariant.
consequence: It decides whether pole placement and feedback design are possible.

title: Kalman Observability Rank Condition
subject: Control Theory
statement: A linear system is observable exactly when the stack of C, CA, ..., CA^(n-1) has full column rank.
short: Outputs must reveal every internal mode.
long: Outputs must reveal every internal mode. Unobservable modes cannot be reconstructed from output histories but may still be stable.
proof: If O loses rank, there is a nonzero initial state producing zero output for all time; conversely the Cayley–Hamilton theorem shows the unobservable subspace is A-invariant.
consequence: It is the dual of controllability and governs state-estimator design.

title: Separation Principle for LQG Control
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear system with Gaussian noise and quadratic cost, an optimal output-feedback controller can be built by combining the optimal state-feedback law with an optimal state estimator, and the two designs can be carried out independently.
latex: u=-K\hat x,\qquad \hat x\ \text{from Kalman filter},\qquad J=J_{\text{LQR}}+J_{\text{est}}
short: Estimate first, then control as if the estimate were exact.
long: Estimate first, then control as if the estimate were exact. The separation property relies on linearity, Gaussianity, and the quadratic cost.
proof: Use dynamic programming and the orthogonality of estimation error to the control history to factor the cost.
consequence: It makes stochastic optimal control computationally tractable.

title: Linear Quadratic Regulator and the Riccati Equation
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear system with quadratic cost, the optimal feedback is u = -Kx where K comes from the stabilizing solution of the algebraic Riccati equation.
short: A matrix quadratic equation encodes the value function.
long: A matrix quadratic equation encodes the value function. Stabilizability and detectability guarantee existence of a unique stabilizing positive semidefinite solution.
proof: Substitute a quadratic value function V=x^TPx into the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation and minimise over u.
consequence: It is the most widely used optimal control design method.

title: Kalman Filter as Optimal Linear Estimator
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear Gaussian state-space model, the Kalman filter recursively computes the conditional mean and covariance of the state given past observations, minimising mean-square error among all estimators.
short: Predict, compare with measurement, and blend by uncertainty.
long: Predict, compare with measurement, and blend by uncertainty. The gain can be interpreted as a least-squares weight between prediction and observation.
proof: Update the Gaussian conditional distribution using Bayes' rule and propagate its covariance through the linear dynamics.
consequence: It is the standard estimator in navigation, tracking, and time-series analysis.

title: Small-Gain Theorem for Feedback Stability
subject: Control Theory
statement: A feedback interconnection of two stable systems is stable if the product of their induced norms is strictly less than one.
short: The loop must not amplify signals around the cycle.
long: The loop must not amplify signals around the cycle. General versions use gains in different induced norms or nonlinear gain functions.
proof: Write the closed-loop equations, take norms, and apply the contraction mapping principle when the loop gain is below one.
consequence: It is a central robust-stability tool for uncertain systems.

title: Lyapunov Equation for Linear Systems
subject: Control Theory
statement: A Hurwitz matrix A admits, for every positive definite Q, a unique positive definite solution P of the Lyapunov equation, and P certifies stability through the quadratic Lyapunov function x^T P x.
short: Solve a linear matrix equation to get a stability certificate.
long: Solve a linear matrix equation to get a stability certificate. The continuous-time and discrete-time versions use different equations.
proof: Take P as an integral of exp(A^T t) Q exp(A t) over positive time and verify the equation by differentiation.
consequence: It provides computationally tractable stability tests and performance bounds.

title: BIBO Stability and Transfer Function Poles
subject: Control Theory
statement: A rational linear time-invariant system is bounded-input bounded-output stable exactly when all poles of its transfer function lie in the open left half-plane.
short: Stable poles mean bounded responses to bounded inputs.
long: Stable poles mean bounded responses to bounded inputs. Unstable pole-zero cancellations can hide internal instability in the transfer function.
proof: The impulse response is a sum of decaying exponentials when poles are stable, so convolution with a bounded input stays bounded.
consequence: It connects time-domain stability with frequency-domain design.

title: Routh–Hurwitz Stability Criterion
subject: Control Theory
statement: A real polynomial has all roots in the open left half-plane exactly when its Hurwitz determinants are all positive, equivalently when the Routh array has no sign changes in its first column.
short: Coefficients alone decide stability.
long: Coefficients alone decide stability. Necessary conditions include all coefficients having the same sign.
proof: Construct the Hurwitz matrix from the coefficients and use the Cauchy index argument relating root locations to the signs of the determinants.
consequence: It tests stability without computing polynomial roots.

title: Nyquist Stability Criterion
subject: Control Theory
statement: The number of unstable poles of a closed-loop system is determined by the winding number of the open-loop frequency response around the point minus one.
short: Count encirclements to count unstable roots.
long: Count encirclements to count unstable roots. The argument principle links the contour integral of the logarithm to zeros and poles.
proof: Apply the argument principle to 1+G(s) along a contour enclosing the right half-plane.
consequence: It provides gain and phase margin information for robust feedback design.

title: Pontryagin Maximum Principle
subject: Control Theory
statement: For an optimal control problem with state and control constraints, an optimal trajectory admits a costate satisfying adjoint equations and a maximisation condition on the Hamiltonian.
short: Optimality is a two-point boundary problem in state and costate.
long: Optimality is a two-point boundary problem in state and costate. For normal problems the costate multiplier on the running cost is negative, and the Hamiltonian is constant when the dynamics are time-invariant.
proof: Apply a variational argument with needle perturbations of the control and use separation of the resulting cones.
consequence: It is the foundational necessary condition for optimal control.

title: Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman Equation
subject: Control Theory
statement: The value function of a continuous-time optimal control problem satisfies a nonlinear first-order PDE obtained by balancing immediate cost against the change in future value.
short: Dynamic programming becomes a partial differential equation.
long: Dynamic programming becomes a partial differential equation. In deterministic quadratic problems it reduces to the Riccati equation; in stochastic settings a second-order term appears.
proof: Apply the dynamic programming principle over a vanishing time step and expand the value function to first order.
consequence: It connects optimal control, viscosity solutions, and reinforcement learning.

title: Complex Exponentials as LTI Eigenfunctions
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Every complex exponential is an eigenfunction of a linear time-invariant system, with eigenvalue given by the system's frequency response.
latex: x(t)=e^{i\omega t}\ \Rightarrow\ y(t)=H(i\omega)e^{i\omega t},\quad H(i\omega)=\int h(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}d\tau
short: Sinusoids pass through LTI systems unchanged except in amplitude and phase.
long: Sinusoids pass through LTI systems unchanged except in amplitude and phase. The frequency response is the Fourier transform of the impulse response when it exists.
proof: Convolve the exponential with the impulse response and use translation to factor out e^{iomega t}.
consequence: Fourier analysis diagonalises LTI filtering and simplifies system design.

title: Butterworth Filter Magnitude Response
subject: Signal Processing
statement: A Butterworth filter has a magnitude response that is maximally flat in the passband and decreases monotonically to zero in the stopband.
short: No ripple in the passband, at the cost of a gentle roll-off.
long: No ripple in the passband, at the cost of a gentle roll-off. The order n sets the steepness; the cutoff omega_c is the half-power point.
proof: Choose a rational response whose first 2n-1 derivatives vanish at zero, giving a polynomial in omega^2 with a triple structure at the origin.
consequence: It is a standard baseline analog filter prototype.

title: Window Functions and Spectral Leakage
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Truncating a signal to a finite record convolves its spectrum with the Fourier transform of the window, spreading energy into neighbouring frequencies.
short: Finite observation smears sharp spectral lines.
long: Finite observation smears sharp spectral lines. Rectangular windows have high sidelobes; Hann and Hamming windows trade resolution for sidelobe suppression.
proof: Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency by the convolution theorem.
consequence: Window choice controls bias and variance in spectral estimation.

title: Wiener Filter and Mean-Square Optimality
subject: Signal Processing
statement: For stationary signal and noise with known spectra, the linear filter minimising mean-square estimation error has a transfer function given by the signal spectrum divided by the total observed spectrum.
short: Pass frequencies where signal dominates noise.
long: Pass frequencies where signal dominates noise. The causal version requires spectral factorisation of the observation spectrum.
proof: Write the mean-square error as an integral, complete the square pointwise in frequency, and choose H accordingly.
consequence: It is the classical optimum benchmark for denoising and equalisation.

title: Least Mean Squares Adaptive Filter
subject: Signal Processing
statement: The LMS algorithm updates filter coefficients by a small multiple of the instantaneous error times the input vector, approximating stochastic gradient descent on mean-square error.
short: Move the weights slightly against the observed error gradient.
long: Move the weights slightly against the observed error gradient. Convergence and misadjustment depend on the step size and input eigenvalue spread.
proof: The instantaneous gradient of the squared error is -2 e_n x_n; taking a single sample gives an unbiased stochastic gradient step.
consequence: It is simple and widely used in echo cancellation and adaptive equalisation.

title: Matched Filter and Signal-to-Noise Ratio
subject: Signal Processing
statement: For detecting a known waveform in additive white noise, the linear filter maximising output signal-to-noise ratio is matched to a time-reversed copy of the signal.
short: Correlate with the signal you expect.
long: Correlate with the signal you expect. The maximum depends on signal energy but not on its detailed shape.
proof: Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the ratio of the filter output at the sampling time to the noise power.
consequence: It is the optimal receiver for known pulses in radar and communications.

title: Multiresolution Analysis and Wavelet Bases
subject: Signal Processing
statement: A multiresolution analysis is a nested sequence of approximation spaces whose differences yield wavelet subspaces, giving orthonormal bases localised in both scale and position.
latex: V_j\subset V_{j+1},\quad V_{j+1}=V_j\oplus W_j,\quad L^2=\bigoplus_j W_j
short: Approximations at one scale plus details at that scale build the next.
long: Approximations at one scale plus details at that scale build the next. Scaling functions generate V_j and wavelets generate W_j through dilation and translation.
proof: Construct the scaling filter satisfying quadrature-mirror conditions and verify orthonormality of the resulting dilates and translates.
consequence: It gives fast wavelet transforms and sparse representations of piecewise-smooth signals.

title: Total Variation Denoising
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Total variation denoising minimises a fidelity term plus a penalty on the total variation of the signal, suppressing noise while preserving sharp edges.
short: Penalise oscillation, not jumps.
long: Penalise oscillation, not jumps. The solution has piecewise-smooth structure; in one dimension it can be computed exactly by the taut-string algorithm.
proof: Convexity gives a unique solution; optimality is expressed by the divergence of a dual field with modulus at most one.
consequence: It is a foundational method in image restoration and inverse problems.

title: Fisher Information Metric on Statistical Manifolds
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Fisher information matrix defines a Riemannian metric on a parametric family of probability distributions, measuring distinguishability of nearby distributions.
short: Statistical distinguishability is a geometric distance.
long: Statistical distinguishability is a geometric distance. It equals the Hessian of the Kullback–Leibler divergence at coinciding parameters.
proof: Expand the KL divergence to second order in the parameter difference and identify the quadratic form.
consequence: It unifies statistics, information theory, and differential geometry.

title: Amari α-Connections and Dually Flat Manifolds
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A statistical manifold carries a one-parameter family of affine connections; the Levi-Civita connection corresponds to alpha zero, while alpha plus or minus one connections make exponential families dually flat.
short: Different connections capture different statistical structures.
long: Different connections capture different statistical structures. Dual flatness yields generalised Pythagorean theorems for divergences.
proof: Verify that the alpha connections are mutually dual with respect to the Fisher metric and that exponential families have vanishing alpha-one curvature.
consequence: It provides the language of information geometry for inference and optimisation.

title: Natural Gradient Descent
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Preconditioning a gradient by the inverse Fisher information makes optimisation steps invariant to reparametrisation of the statistical model.
short: Move a fixed distance in distribution space, not parameter space.
long: Move a fixed distance in distribution space, not parameter space. It approximates steepest descent with respect to the Fisher–Rao metric.
proof: The Fisher metric transforms covariantly under reparametrisation, so the inverse-metric gradient transforms as a tangent vector.
consequence: It improves conditioning in probabilistic models and reinforcement learning.
